text: Every field a requester fills in on a catalog item's order form — which laptop model, a business justification, a preferred start date — is a variable. As the administrator, you define the question itself once on item_option_new: its label, its type, its help text, and any conditions controlling it. Each time a real requester actually submits the form, their specific answer is captured as a separate record on sc_item_option.

ServiceNow ships a fixed set of real variable types. Single Line Text and Multi Line Text handle short and long free text. Choice offers an admin-defined dropdown; Multiple Choice lets a requester pick more than one option. Reference points to an actual record on another table instead of accepting typed text. Checkbox and Yes/No capture a two-state answer, and Lookup Select Box can auto-populate other variables from a lookup.

Picking the right type isn't cosmetic. A Reference variable pointed at sys_user guarantees the requested-for answer is a real, valid user record that approvals and workflows can act on. A Single Line Text variable asking the same question would let someone type a name with a typo that no approval step could ever resolve, breaking the automation built on top of it.

Now picture ten catalog items that all need to ask who a request is really for, and what cost center to bill. Defining those two variables separately on all ten items means ten separate places to fix a typo or add a new cost center option. A Variable Set groups a group of variables together once — commonly something like Requester Info — and that one set attaches to as many catalog items as need it.

A one-to-one variable set is reused across many items sharing the same fields. A multi-row variable set lets a requester add several repeated rows of the same group of variables on one form — useful for adding one row per additional attendee on an event-registration item. Not every variable belongs in a set: something genuinely unique to a single item, like a specific room number, stays directly on that item.

The practical test: if you're ever copying a variable's configuration from one catalog item to another by hand, that variable should have lived in a shared set from the start. Next up: Catalog UI Policies, which control how these very variables behave — showing, hiding, or requiring them based on a requester's other answers.
